scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

When faced with a tough decision, you ask: > * " *Would this satisfy Allah?*" > * " *Does this reflect the Prophet’s (ﷺ) character?*" This isn’t about fear—it’s about * love and respect*. The Hadith where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: > * " *None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself* " (Bukhari) becomes a practical filter for every interaction. - ** it’s not just " rules" but * character-building***: The Quran doesn’t just say " don’t lie"— it teaches * why* truthfulness matters (e.g., Quran 33:70-71 on " *sincerity in speech*"). This shapes * who you are*, not just what you do. --- ### **3. It Connects You to a Living Tradition** - ** you’re not alone in this journey**: When you return to the Quran, you’re joining a 1,400-year conversation of scholars, saints, and ordinary Muslims who’ve wrestled with the same questions. Tafsir (Quranic commentary) and Hadith sciences exist precisely to help us * understand context*—so you’re not just reading words, but * engaging with a wisdom tradition*. - ** it prevents isolation in decision-making**: In a world where " *my truth* " often dominates, the Quran reminds us: > * " *... and consult them in affairs* " (Quran 3:159) This encourages seeking counsel from knowledgeable people * while* grounding your own judgment in divine guidance. --- ### **4. It Changes * How* You Think** - ** from " *What do I want?*" to " *What is right?*"**: The Quran trains the mind to prioritize * justice ( adl)*, * compassion ( rahmah)*, and * truth ( haqq)* over personal desires. Example: > * " *... do not let hatred of a people incite you to aggression* " (Quran 5:2) This isn’t just about avoiding revenge—it’s a * mental discipline* to see beyond emotion. - ** it’s a " * spiritual workout* "**: Just as physical exercise builds strength, regularly returning to the Quran builds * moral resilience*. Over time, its principles become instinctive. You start * automatically* asking: > * " *Does this align with the Quranic ideal of a just society?*" > * " *Would the Prophet (ﷺ) have handled this with patience and wisdom?*" --- ### **A Crucial Note: humility in interpretation** While this practice is powerful, it’s also why ** seeking knowledge** matters. The Quran itself says: > * " *... ask those who know if you do not know* " (Quran 16:43) - ** avoid " * cherry-picking* " verses out of context**. A verse about patience (e.g., 2:153) shouldn’t be used to justify staying in an abusive situation—because the Quran also commands * self-respect and justice*. - ** balance revelation with reason ( *‘aqeel*)**. Islam encourages critical thinking (e.g., Quran 2:164 on " *reflecting on creation*"). The Hadith where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: > * " *Wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he has the right to it* " (Tirmidhi) means * all* truth ( scientific, ethical, practical) can complement divine guidance. --- ### **Final Thought** What you’re doing is ** not just a ritual—it’s a daily realignment of your soul with truth**. It’s like having a compass that points to * true north* in a world full of magnetic distractions. Over time, this practice doesn’t just * help* you decide what’s right—it * reshapes* your entire being to * embody* what’s right. prediction.raw: **0 (NTA - Not the Asshole)** **Why:** - **Your savings are YOURS.** You’ve been saving from *your own earnings* for a *personal goal* (post-graduation vacation). This is not " family money" or a shared resource—it’s your hard-earned, discipline-driven savings. - **Your brother is an adult with financial responsibility.** At 30, he’s living rent-free, has a job, and *chose* to go back to school. His "horrible with money" habits (despite similar income to yours) are *his* issue, not yours. He should be saving for himself, not relying on you. - **His " unfairness" arguments don’t hold up:** - " * Parents spoiled me*" is subjective and irrelevant. You didn’t choose your circumstances, and your saving came from *your* discipline (your dad and university taught you budgeting, not " spoiling"). - " * I got to go on trips while he didn’t*" is a non sequitur. You saved for *your* future; he didn’t save for *his*. That’s on him, not you. - " * I’ll pay you back*" is unreliable when he’s proven financially irresponsible. $2800 is a significant sum for you to risk on a gamble. - **Boundaries are healthy.** Refusing to loan money to someone with a history of poor financial management is ** responsible self-preservation**, not " being a jerk." - **Your parents were right:** They told him * he* should save for himself ( " * he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year*"). That’s the correct approach—he’s an adult who needs to take ownership of his finances. **Key takeaway:** You’re not obligated to fund your brother’s vacation, especially when he’s shown he can’t manage his own money. Your refusal protects your goals and teaches him accountability. **This is 100% reasonable.** *(If he’s truly struggling, suggest he get a part-time job or seek financial counseling—but that’s his problem to solve, not yours.)* **Final verdict: NTA (0)**. You did the right thing. 💡
